headline: After eight years and nine planetary flybys, BepiColombo has reached Mercury
dek: The European-Japanese mission is beginning its capture into orbit around the smallest planet, which only one spacecraft has orbited before. Its X-ray telescope has already passed its first test on a distant nebula.
body: Getting into orbit around Mercury is harder than it sounds. The planet sits deep in the Sun's gravity well, so a spacecraft falling toward it picks up enormous speed that has to be shed before it can stay. BepiColombo, a joint mission of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), has spent eight years doing exactly that, and 21 November 2026 is the date set for its capture by Mercury's gravity.
Only one spacecraft has orbited Mercury before: NASA's MESSENGER, from 2011 to 2015. BepiColombo will be the first mission to put two orbiters around the planet at the same time.

BepiColombo launched in October 2018 as a stack of three craft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, known as Mio, and a propulsion stage called the Mercury Transfer Module. To lose speed it swung past Earth once, Venus twice and Mercury six times.

The trip did not go to plan. In 2024 a power fault stopped the transfer module's electric thrusters from running at full strength, and the team had to redesign the route. That pushed arrival back from December 2025 to November 2026 and meant flying just 165 kilometres above Mercury on the fourth flyby, closer than the 200 kilometres originally treated as safe. The transfer module was released on 3 September 2026, its job done.

body.quote: "For the first time, we'll have a single mission with two orbiters going around the same planet." (Geraint Jones, ESA BepiColombo project scientist, via IFLScience)

body: Capture is only the start. ESA has planned a series of engine burns running into early 2027 to shape the orbits. MPO and Mio are due to separate on 9 and 10 December. Mio will settle into a stretched orbit lasting about nine hours to study Mercury's magnetic field and its thin wisp of an atmosphere, while MPO lowers itself into a tighter loop of about two and a half hours to map the surface. Science operations are scheduled to begin in April 2027.

There is plenty to explain. Mercury's iron core reaches about 85 per cent of the way to the surface, a far bigger share than Earth's. The planet has a global magnetic field, though a weak one, and it is slowly shrinking as it cools. Its permanently shadowed polar craters appear to hold ice, and its surface is pocked with odd shallow pits called hollows that MESSENGER found but could not fully explain.

One instrument is already showing what it can do. The Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), built by a consortium led by the University of Leicester in the UK, is the first imaging X-ray telescope sent on a planetary mission. It will map which chemical elements make up Mercury's rocks by catching the X-rays they give off when the Sun's X-rays strike them. In a 39-hour calibration run on 11 and 12 September it observed the Crab Nebula, about 6,500 light-years away, and produced images slightly sharper than in its 2015 laboratory tests, with no stray light and no sign of radiation damage to its detector.

body.quote: "MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space!" (Emma Bunce, MIXS principal investigator, University of Leicester, via Phys.org)

body: Some instrument effects are still being studied, and all the dates after capture are plans that could shift. The first real science from Mercury's orbit is still months away.

headline: A dead star is beaming radio pulses every eight minutes, and its partner looks a lot like our Sun
dek: Australian astronomers traced a repeating radio signal to a white dwarf circling a Sun-like star. The pulses are clean enough to follow the dead star around its orbit, and they even picked up a storm on its companion.
body: Since 2021, radio astronomers have been finding a strange kind of signal: sources that switch on and off on a cycle of minutes to hours, much slower than ordinary pulsars. About a dozen of these long-period transients are now known, and what powers them is still debated. A study published on 12 November in Nature Astronomy pins one of them on a pairing nobody had seen before: a white dwarf orbiting a star much like the Sun.

The source is called GPM J071507−114153. It flashes about every 7.9 minutes, which the team takes to be the spin of the white dwarf, the Earth-sized leftover core of a dead star. The research was led by Sam McSweeney, who did the work at the Curtin University node of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) and is now a commissioning scientist at the SKA Observatory, with Natasha Hurley-Walker and colleagues.

body.h2: From a sky survey to one faint star

body: The signal turned up in a survey of the Milky Way made with the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) in Western Australia. Doctoral student Csanád Horváth developed the search method that flagged it, and the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre processed more than 100 hours of observations. The MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa then narrowed the position to a tiny patch of sky containing a single faint star. Spectra from the Keck I telescope in Hawaii showed it to be a G-type star, with a temperature and mass close to the Sun's.

That was a surprise. Earlier long-period transients with a white dwarf involved small, cool red dwarfs, and in those systems it was unclear which star made the pulses. Here the arrival times of the pulses shift by up to a few seconds as the white dwarf swings around its partner, which places the source at or near the white dwarf.

body.quote: "This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion." (Sam McSweeney, SKA Observatory, via Space.com)

body.h2: A storm seen through radio light

body: The pulses are also modulated on a cycle of about 1.3 days, which the team reads as the orbital period of the two stars. They are visible for roughly six hours of each orbit and then fade. As the white dwarf passed behind its companion, the polarisation of its pulses changed quickly, which the authors link to the radio waves crossing the Sun-like star's hot outer atmosphere. The team says one episode was most likely a prominence, a huge loop of magnetised gas thrown up from the star's surface, similar to the flares on the Sun that drive auroras on Earth.

The researchers place the system more than 5,000 light-years away. Some coverage gave a figure closer to 10,000 light-years; the paper's own distance estimate was not available to us, so the exact value should be treated as uncertain. Timing also suggests the Sun-like star is not overflowing onto the white dwarf, so the radio beam seems to need some other kind of interaction between the two.

One system cannot settle what powers all long-period transients, and the authors note the class may contain more than one type of object. The MWA and MeerKAT are forerunners of the Square Kilometre Array telescopes being built in Australia and South Africa, which the team expects to find many more.

headline: Dust grains caught high above Earth carry traces of ancient ice from beyond Neptune
dek: NASA scientists studied 12 microscopic particles collected in the stratosphere. Their minerals were altered by water rich in heavy oxygen, a signature that is rare in meteorites.
location: NASA Johnson Space Center, United States
body: Thousands of tonnes of cosmic dust settle onto Earth every year, and NASA has spent decades catching some of it with high-altitude aircraft such as the ER-2. In a study published in Science Advances, researchers led by Lindsay Keller at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston report that a handful of these grains came from the Kuiper Belt, the icy zone beyond Neptune, and that they preserve the fingerprint of water unlike the water recorded in most meteorites.

The team examined 12 particles, each 10 to 30 micrometres across, using electron microscopes at Johnson and an ion microprobe at the University of California, Los Angeles, an instrument that measures isotopes in tiny samples.

To work out where a grain came from, the researchers counted tracks left in it by energetic particles from the Sun. The longer a grain drifts through space, the more of these tracks it collects, and dust from the far reaches of the solar system spends a long time spiralling inward. These 12 carried roughly 100 times as many tracks as expected for dust from the asteroid belt or from comets in Jupiter's family, which points to the Kuiper Belt. In 2022, Keller and George Flynn of the State University of New York estimated that up to a quarter of the interplanetary dust reaching the inner solar system may come from there.

Inside, the grains are dominated by clays such as saponite and serpentine and other minerals that form only when rock reacts with fluids, in this case water mixed with carbon dioxide at low temperatures. They are also rich in carbon, about four times more than some carbon-rich meteorites. The authors suggest the starting material was glassy silicate grains dotted with tiny specks of iron-nickel metal and sulfides.

body.h2: Heavy water from a separate store

body: Oxygen comes in three stable forms: oxygen-16, oxygen-17 and oxygen-18. The grains are enriched in the two heavier ones, which means the water that altered them was too. Using chemical models, the team estimates that the original water's ratio of oxygen-18 to oxygen-16 was up to roughly 15 percent above that of Earth's ocean water. That figure is an upper limit worked out from the minerals, because the water itself is long gone.

Scientists have expected ice like this in the outer solar system, where light-driven chemistry is thought to have pushed heavy oxygen into ice. NASA's Genesis mission supported the idea when it found that the Sun holds proportionally more light oxygen than Earth and most meteorites. But hard evidence was scarce, limited to hints in one primitive meteorite and in comet 67P.

body.quote: "Compelling evidence for the presence of a major heavy water reservoir beyond the orbits of the gas giant planets." (Lindsay Keller and colleagues, NASA Johnson Space Center, in Science Advances)

body: Because the signature is so rare in meteorites, the team argues that this outer store of ice barely mixed with material closer to the Sun. They point to Saturn, and perhaps Uranus and Neptune, as a possible barrier: simulations predict a zone of higher gas pressure just outside Saturn's orbit in the solar system's first few million years, which could have stopped outer dust from drifting inward.

The study rests on just 12 grains, and their Kuiper Belt origin is inferred from track counts rather than traced directly. The isotope value is a model-based upper limit, and the giant-planet barrier is a hypothesis drawn from simulations. With no way to sample the Kuiper Belt directly for now, dust that falls to Earth remains one of the few windows onto it.

headline: Euclid's first big data haul maps 900 million galaxies, and it covers only 14% of the job
dek: ESA's dark-universe telescope has opened 13 months of survey data, including about 15,000 possible gravitational lenses. The measurements needed for cosmology arrive in 2027.
body: Euclid, the European Space Agency telescope launched in July 2023 to study dark matter and dark energy, released its first large batch of survey data on 12 November. Called DR1-Foundation, it covers about 13 months of observations, from spring 2024 to spring 2025, and serves as a preview: the complete first data release is due in mid-2027.

The release spans roughly 1,900 square degrees of sky, an area equal to about 9,500 full Moons, and takes in light from more than a billion objects. Among them are more than 900 million galaxies, over 60 million candidate quasars (the bright cores of galaxies whose central black holes are feeding), and spectra for more than 160 million sources, which help astronomers pin down distances and chemical makeup. The whole package comes to about 1.7 petabytes, built from around 10,000 science images taken by Euclid's visible-light camera, VIS, and its near-infrared instrument, NISP.
For comparison, Euclid's earlier public data covered just a few days of observations over about 60 square degrees.

body.quote: "These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos." (Carole Mundell, ESA Director of Science, via Phys.org)

body: When a massive galaxy sits in front of a more distant one, its gravity bends and magnifies the light from behind, sometimes into arcs or complete rings. These strong gravitational lenses let astronomers weigh the foreground galaxy, dark matter included, and spot faint galaxies that would otherwise be out of reach. DR1-Foundation contains about 15,000 lens candidates, found with a mix of machine learning, visual checks and help from citizen scientists. That is more than all earlier lens catalogues put together.

body.quote: "Before Euclid, we had fewer than 1,000 confirmed strong lenses. Now we have 15,000 new candidates." (Hrishabh Srivastava, University of British Columbia, via Phys.org)

body: Over its planned six-year survey, Euclid is expected to turn up more than 100,000 strong lenses.

Dark matter and dark energy together account for about 95% of the universe's matter and energy, yet neither has been directly detected. Euclid's plan is to chart billions of galaxies across roughly a third of the sky, measuring how their shapes are slightly warped by matter along the line of sight (weak lensing) and how they cluster. Together with distances, that builds a 3D map of how the cosmic web grew over time, which is where the effects of the dark components should show up.

This release covers only about 14% of the area the full survey will map, and the lens candidates still need follow-up observations to confirm them. The higher-level weak-lensing and galaxy-clustering products, which the first dark energy measurements will depend on, are not part of it; ESA says they will be published in mid-2027 to complete Data Release 1, with cosmology results to follow. More than 2,500 researchers at over 300 institutions in the Euclid Consortium are already working with the data.

headline: An AI that had never seen a black hole was asked to image M87*. It drew the same ring
dek: Astronomers at CSIRO rebuilt the famous Event Horizon Telescope picture from public data, using a method that avoids calibration errors and assumes nothing about black holes. The ring came back the same size.
body: In April 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration showed the world its first picture of a black hole: a lopsided ring of light around M87*, the giant black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87, some 55 million light-years away. A small team at CSIRO, Australia's national science agency, has now rebuilt that picture from the same public data with a method of its own, and the ring is still there. The work was published in Nature on 11 November.

Why check at all? The EHT links radio dishes across the planet into one Earth-sized telescope, but it only samples the sky at scattered points, so any picture has to be reconstructed from incomplete information. The original image came from four separate imaging teams. All four found a ring, yet they disagreed on finer features, and a few outside reanalyses went further and questioned whether the ring was real or a side effect of processing choices.

The CSIRO approach, led by astronomer Samuel Lai with project leader Nithyanandan Thyagarajan, tackles two weak spots. First, instead of working with pairs of telescopes, it combines measurements from three or more at a time into quantities called closure invariants. In those combinations, many errors added by Earth's atmosphere and by individual telescopes cancel out, so the result does not hinge on how each dish was calibrated.

Second, the images are produced by a machine-learning tool the team built, called GenDIReCT. It was trained on everyday pictures such as cats, dogs and cars rather than on simulated black holes, so it had no built-in expectation of a ring. The team tested it on shapes that are not rings and on real data from another galaxy, Centaurus A, and froze its settings before running it on M87*, to keep their own expectations out of the result.

body.quote: "This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process." (Samuel Lai, CSIRO, via Phys.org)

body: The team used the publicly released EHT measurements from 2017, 2018 and 2021, eight observing nights in all. Every dataset produced a compact ring. On the best night of each year the ring had a consistent size and orientation, and the team measured its diameter at 42.2 millionths of an arcsecond, give or take 1.5. That fits a black hole of about 6.5 billion times the Sun's mass, seen roughly 20 degrees from the direction of its jet, in line with the EHT's own results. A more traditional statistical imaging method, run on the same triplet-based data, backed up the shape.

The ring's orientation also shifted between the 2017 and 2018 observations, which the authors attribute to the turbulent flow of gas around the black hole. Some of the change seen within 2017 itself may instead come from the patchier coverage on two of that year's nights.

body.quote: "Independent validation is at the heart of the scientific process." (Laurent Loinard, director of the EHT Collaboration, via Space.com)

body: The agreement is about the overall shape. The new images differ from the EHT's in finer details, such as the thickness of the ring and how its brightness varies around the circle, and on a few lower-quality nights the reconstructions were less clean. Because the study reuses the EHT's own observations, it checks how the image was made rather than offering a new look at the black hole. Thyagarajan says the triplet technique might one day help in other fields, such as medical imaging or earthquake mapping, but that has not been tried yet.

headline: Two giant black holes were already feeding side by side 900 million years after the Big Bang
dek: Webb spotted a second quasar hiding next to a known one, and Gemini North split the pair apart. It is the most compact quasar pair yet found from cosmic dawn, and its black holes are bigger than theory comfortably allows.
location: NSF NOIRLab / International Gemini Observatory, United States
body: A quasar is a supermassive black hole swallowing gas so fast that the material around it outshines its whole galaxy. Finding even one in the young universe raises the question of how such a heavy object grew so quickly. Astronomers have now found two of them close together, seen as they were roughly 900 million years after the Big Bang, when the universe was about a thirteenth of its present age.

The pair is catalogued as J1602+4228AB and has been given the Hawaiian name Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua. The study, led by Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral researcher at NSF NOIRLab and the International Gemini Observatory, appears in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

body.h2: Webb found it, Gemini split it

body: The second quasar showed up during a visual check of data from Aether, a survey led by Emanuele Paolo Farina of NOIRLab/Gemini that uses the NIRSpec instrument on the James Webb Space Telescope. Aether has gathered spectra of about 200 quasars, which the team says is 43% of those known from that era. In the data for one known quasar, J1602+4228A, the team noticed a companion. Earlier ground-based images had shown the two as a single source.

Follow-up with the GNIRS spectrograph on the Gemini North telescope on Maunakea, Hawaii, resolved the two quasars as separate objects. Onorato said the sky was clear and steady enough that the data took only two nights. A second Gemini instrument, GMOS, was used to test whether the fainter quasar might be a mirror image of the brighter one, created by a foreground galaxy bending its light.

body.quote: "There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early." (Silvia Onorato, NSF NOIRLab, via Phys.org)

body: According to the paper, the two quasars sit at a redshift of about 6.08 and lie just under one arcsecond apart on the sky, which works out to about 5.6 kiloparsecs, or roughly 18,100 light-years. That is around a fifth of the width of the Milky Way. Their black holes weigh about 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun, and both are taking in matter at or slightly above the rate usually thought of as a natural limit.

It is only the third quasar pair known from this early period and the most compact. The authors compared its existence with how strongly early quasars are expected to cluster, and found that a pair this close should be hundreds to thousands of times rarer than it appears to be. They suggest either that galaxy mergers in the young universe often switched on two quasars at once, or that this pair lives in an unusually crowded region.

Caveats remain. The paper calls the system a candidate pair: the GMOS spectra of the two sources differ, which favours two real quasars, but the team says a model of possible gravitational lensing is still needed to rule out a single quasar seen twice. A single system is also too few to say how common such pairs were.

headline: A tiny asteroid is drifting off course, and the hidden-ice explanation just got harder to believe
dek: Asteroid 1998 KY26 is being nudged by something other than gravity. New thermal simulations suggest it is far too warm to hold the buried ice that would make it a 'dark comet', and Japan has just called off its probe's visit.
location: Georgia Institute of Technology, United States
body: Asteroid 1998 KY26 is small even by asteroid standards. Observations with the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope in 2024 showed it is only about 11 metres wide, three to four times smaller than earlier estimates, and that it completes a full turn in roughly five and a half minutes. That makes it one of the fastest-spinning asteroids known.

It also moves in a way gravity alone does not explain. A 2023 analysis of its orbit found a small but statistically significant push, including a component sideways out of the plane of its orbit around the Sun. KY26 was one of six near-Earth objects in that study with this kind of unexplained drift, and the authors floated the idea that they might be "dark comets": bodies that release gas, like a comet, but too faintly to show a visible tail or fuzzy coma.

A study by Korbin Hansen and Masatoshi Hirabayashi of the Georgia Institute of Technology, published in the journal Icarus, put that idea to a direct test. The pair built a three-dimensional thermal model of KY26 and tracked how hot its surface and interior get over a full orbit. They ran 13 versions, changing the asteroid's size, how much light it reflects, how well its rock conducts heat and which way its spin axis points.

For water ice to last in the vacuum of space over long periods, it has to stay below about 145 kelvin, or around minus 128 degrees Celsius. In every version of the model, even the coldest parts of KY26 averaged more than 60 degrees warmer than that. No sheltered pocket, on the surface or deep inside, stayed cold enough.

body.quote: "The water outgassing rate on 1998 KY26 would be too high to maintain buried ice." (Korbin Hansen and Masatoshi Hirabayashi, Georgia Institute of Technology, via ScienceAlert)

body: Even if ice once made up 1 per cent of the asteroid's mass, the model suggests it would all be gone in about 2,000 years, a blink in the life of an asteroid. The authors conclude a dark comet is highly unlikely. They favour a gentler explanation: the pressure of sunlight hitting the asteroid, combined with the heat its surface radiates back into space, which can add up to a noticeable shove on something this small and light. Earlier measurements of reflected light also point to a bright, rocky body with little water.

The best way to settle the question would have been to go and look. KY26 was the final target of JAXA's Hayabusa2, the probe that brought samples of asteroid Ryugu back to Earth in 2020, with a rendezvous planned for 2031. On 17 November JAXA said it was dropping that plan after a problem with the spacecraft's ion engines was found in August. Hayabusa2 will instead make a fast, close flyby of a different small asteroid, 2015 BM510, in April 2028, with no landing.

A fringe idea has also been aired: Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb has proposed that KY26 is a lost Soviet spacecraft. Coverage of that claim notes it relies on an engine burn for which there is no evidence, and it is not supported by other researchers.

The new study has limits. It is a model, built on what little is known about KY26, and the asteroid's past orbit is uncertain, so the authors do not rule out every trace of ice. It also tests one explanation rather than measuring what is actually pushing the asteroid.

headline: A giant planet stopped crossing its star while TESS was watching, and an unseen neighbour is to blame
dek: For seven years NASA's TESS saw the hot Jupiter TOI-2535 b pass in front of its star. Then the crossings shrank and stopped. Astronomers say the pull of a second, hidden giant planet has tipped its orbit out of line with Earth.
location: University of California, Los Angeles, United States
body: Most of the planets known beyond the Solar System were found because they pass in front of their star and dim it slightly once per orbit. That trick depends on luck: the orbit has to be lined up almost edge-on to Earth. A study published on 9 November in The Astrophysical Journal Letters describes the first confirmed planet around a single star whose crossings have been seen to fade out and stop altogether.

The planet is TOI-2535 b, a hot Jupiter with roughly the mass of Jupiter that circles its star every 8.24 days, far closer in than Mercury sits to the Sun. Its host is an old orange dwarf, a little less massive than the Sun and about 9.7 billion years old, roughly 1,100 light-years from Earth. The work was led by Samuel Yee, a 51 Pegasi b Fellow at UCLA, with Erik Petigura and an international team.

NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) looked at the system in five stretches between April 2019 and March 2026. Almost nothing about the planet's crossings stayed constant. They arrived up to about six hours earlier or later than a steady orbit would predict, one of the largest timing swings known for a hot Jupiter. Each crossing also got shorter and shallower, a sign that the planet's path was sliding toward the edge of the star's disc. In the last TESS look, in early 2026, no crossing showed up at all.

Ground-based telescopes in the Las Cumbres Observatory network and at several smaller observatories caught extra crossings along the way. The NEID spectrograph on the WIYN telescope at Kitt Peak, Arizona, measured the star's wobble to confirm that the object is a planet and not a second star.

body.quote: "The planet's orbit is tilting so quickly that its transit disappeared while we were watching." (Samuel Yee, UCLA, via Space.com)

body.h2: A hidden partner doing the tilting

body: The planet is not gone, and nothing went wrong with the telescope. Its orbit is slowly swivelling, like a spinning top that wobbles. When the team modelled the timing and shape changes together, the best explanation was a second planet nearby, orbiting on a plane tilted at least about 5 degrees from the first. Their gravity makes both orbits precess, with one full cycle taking roughly 30 to 50 years. That means TOI-2535 b should start crossing its star again within a few decades.

The hidden neighbour has not been seen directly. Its existence is inferred from its gravitational effects. The models suggest it is at least as massive as Saturn and probably locked in a regular rhythm with the hot Jupiter, most likely completing two orbits for every one of TOI-2535 b's, or three for every two. The exact mass, period and tilt are not yet pinned down, and the leftover scatter in the data hints that more than one unseen planet could be involved. The authors say a dense campaign of star-wobble measurements is now the best way to find it.

The system also matters for how hot Jupiters end up so close to their stars. A giant planet with a close giant neighbour probably did not get flung inward on a wild, stretched orbit. It more likely drifted in slowly through the disc of gas it formed in. Such discs tend to leave planets in flat systems, though, so something must have tilted these two orbits later, and what did it is still an open question.

headline: Earth has had a second moon since spring, and it is only about the size of a person
dek: A tiny asteroid called 2026 QQ8 was pulled into a loose loop around Earth in April. Astronomers confirmed it is a natural rock, not space junk, and it is due to slip away within weeks.
location: IAU Minor Planet Center, United States
body: On the night of 19 to 20 August, Hungarian astronomer Krisztián Sárneczky picked up a faint moving dot in images from the Piszkéstető mountain station in Hungary. Follow-up tracking showed it was not passing Earth on its own path around the Sun. It was going around Earth.

The object, now designated 2026 QQ8, is a temporary mini-moon: a small asteroid briefly held by Earth's gravity before the Sun's pull takes it away again. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center announced it on 29 October in an electronic circular titled "Temporarily Captured Object".

body.quote: "Orbit integrations indicate that this object is temporarily bound to the Earth." (Minor Planet Center, MPEC 2026-U95)

body: Small things circling Earth are often spent rocket stages, so the first question was whether 2026 QQ8 is natural. In early September even orbit-watchers were unsure. The Minor Planet Center's circular settled it as far as current data allow: its orbit fit, which includes the small push from sunlight, found no link to any known artificial object, and it is listed as a natural asteroid.

It is very small. Its brightness puts it at roughly 1 to 3 metres across, depending on how reflective its surface is; Live Science, citing the IAU, gives about 2 metres. A rock that size poses no danger. If it ever did hit the atmosphere it would most likely break up and burn as a bright fireball.

Orbit calculations from NASA's JPL suggest 2026 QQ8 drifted into Earth's neighbourhood in April and passed about 1.2 million kilometres from Earth on 1 May before being caught. Its closest pass so far came on 18 August, at roughly 537,000 kilometres, about 1.4 times the Moon's distance, the day before it was spotted.

The stay will be brief. JPL's orbit shows one more pass on 13 December at around 1.35 million kilometres, after which it should break free. Coverage differs slightly on timing, from mid-December to January 2027. Around the Sun, the asteroid takes 359 days per lap, almost exactly a year, so it keeps returning near Earth about once a decade. The next close approach in the current orbit solution is in 2058.

body.h2: Not the first, and not the last

body: Earth has caught visitors like this before. 2006 RH120, a few metres wide, circled for about a year in 2006 and 2007. 2020 CD3, discovered in February 2020, had been bound for more than a year before it left that spring. 2024 PT5, about 10 metres across, stayed for roughly two months in late 2024, and its colour suggests it may be a chip knocked off the Moon. Researchers think Earth holds at least one tiny mini-moon at most times; most are simply too small and faint to find.

Its size is an estimate, since nobody has measured it directly, and its exit date depends on an orbit based on about three months of observations. New survey telescopes such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile are expected to catch many more of these brief companions.

headline: A star smaller than the Sun spiralled into a supergiant, and Webb caught the aftermath
dek: In the Andromeda galaxy, astronomers followed a two-star system called Bao as the smaller star sank into its bloated partner. The final plunge took about seven years instead of the thousands of orbits seen in other mergers.
body: Stars that orbit each other closely can end up as one. Astronomers have long pieced such mergers together after the fact, from the glowing debris they leave behind. A study published in Nature on 18 November describes a merger that was followed while it was happening, in a system in the Andromeda galaxy, our large neighbour about 2.5 million light-years away.

The event is catalogued as AT 2025abao, and the team nicknamed it Bao. Before the merger, the bigger star ("Big Bao") was a puffed-up supergiant of about seven times the Sun's mass, some 350 times wider than the Sun and roughly 18,000 times brighter. Its companion ("Little Bao") was a modest star of about 0.7 solar masses, a little smaller and dimmer than our own.

body.h2: A slow build-up, then a fast ending

body: Several telescopes picked up the warning signs. Archival data from NASA's NEOWISE mission show the system shining steadily until 2018, then varying by early 2023. A ground-based infrared survey called WINTER saw it brighten and make dust in 2024, and NASA's SPHEREx mission recorded it fading in visible light while growing brighter in the infrared in mid-2025. On 17 October 2025 the Zwicky Transient Facility in California spotted the eruption itself, and Swift and the Gemini North telescope followed up.

The James Webb Space Telescope looked on 24 December 2025, 47 days after the outburst peaked, under a fast-track observing slot. Lead author Viraj Karambelkar, a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University, says no event of this kind has been followed up that early. Webb's mid-infrared view recorded dust the system had shed over centuries, which let the team test computer models of the merger.

body.quote: "Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict." (Viraj Karambelkar, Columbia University, via Phys.org)

body: In the models, which were led by Karel Temmink at Radboud University in the Netherlands, the small star slipped into the outer layers of the supergiant, a stage astronomers call a common envelope. It then sank toward the core within about seven orbits, or roughly seven years. Mergers seen before between two smaller stars dragged on for thousands of orbits. Team member Kishalay De of Columbia compared the encounter to a bomb going off inside a living star.

The researchers say it is the first time a smaller star has been seen merging with a bloated supergiant, and that catching it early let them estimate how much material was thrown off. They expect NASA's upcoming Roman Space Telescope to find many more events like it.

There are limits. The masses and sizes of both stars come from models matched to the data, not from direct measurements. What the merged star looks like now, and how its mass will settle, is still unknown and will need further observations. Not every close pair ends this way: in some systems both stars survive on a tight orbit.

headline: Europe's Hera probe has reached the asteroid pair NASA deliberately rammed in 2022
dek: ESA's first planetary defence spacecraft has sent back its first close-up of Didymos, the bigger partner of the moonlet DART struck. The real crash-site investigation starts now.
body: In September 2022, NASA flew a spacecraft straight into a small asteroid on purpose to see whether a collision could push it off course. Four years later, a European probe has arrived to inspect the scene. ESA's Hera spacecraft reached the Didymos asteroid system in November 2026, about a month ahead of its original schedule, and ESA released its first close-up image on 5 November.

Didymos is roughly 780 metres across. A much smaller moonlet, Dimorphos, about 150 metres wide, circles it at a distance of around a kilometre. Neither poses any threat to Earth, which is why the pair was chosen for the test.

NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft, which weighed about 580 kilograms, hit Dimorphos on 26 September 2022 at roughly 6 kilometres per second. The impact cut the time Dimorphos takes to orbit Didymos by about 33 minutes, a much bigger change than scientists had expected. It was the first time people had measurably changed the path of a natural object in the Solar System.

What DART could not reveal was the full aftermath: the size of the crater, how much rock was blasted away, and the masses and internal makeup of the two asteroids. Those details matter for working out how hard you would need to hit a more dangerous asteroid to nudge it aside. Hera's job is to fill those gaps.

Hera launched on 7 October 2024 and used a flyby of Mars in March 2025 to bend its path toward Didymos. Its first close-up, taken with its black-and-white Asteroid Framing Camera, shows a world covered in boulders and craters, with a ridge around its equator and patterns of grooves. Dimorphos sits mostly in shadow, so the DART impact site is not yet visible.

body.quote: "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact." (Patrick Michel, Hera principal investigator, via Popular Science)

body: One open question is whether debris thrown off Dimorphos crossed the short gap and landed on Didymos, adding to the features in the new picture. ESA mission scientist Michael Kueppers said the team has exciting work ahead to sort that out.

These are first-look images, not scientific results. Over the coming months Hera is due to map both asteroids in detail, and it carries two suitcase-sized CubeSats, Milani and Juventas, for even closer looks. ESA has said sharper images of Didymos and Dimorphos will follow on 25 November.

headline: One nuclear blast in orbit could disable almost every low-orbit satellite within a week, model suggests
dek: A simulation of a single one-megaton detonation found that an artificial radiation belt would wear down roughly 98% of more than 13,000 satellites in seven days. The study is a preprint and has not yet been peer reviewed.
body: Thousands of satellites now circle close to Earth, carrying internet links, imaging, weather data and navigation support. A new modelling study asks what would happen to them if a nuclear weapon went off in their midst. Its answer: the explosion itself would do limited harm, but what it leaves behind could take out almost all of them.

The work was led by Zachary Petersen, an undergraduate at the University of Wisconsin–Madison, with co-authors Hong Qin, Sarah Thiele and Sébastien Philippe, and involved researchers at Princeton University. It was posted on the preprint server arXiv on 6 November and has not yet been through peer review.

The team simulated a one-megaton bomb detonated 500 kilometres above the South Atlantic, near a region where Earth's magnetic field is weak, known as the South Atlantic Anomaly. They used real orbital data for roughly 13,300 satellites active in low Earth orbit in January 2026.

In the model, the initial flash of radiation disabled only about 3% of them. The bigger danger came afterwards. Radioactive debris from the blast releases electrons that get caught in Earth's magnetic field, forming an artificial radiation belt. Every time a satellite passes through it, it absorbs another dose, until its electronics fail. About a quarter were out of action after one day, 78% after three days and roughly 98% after a week.

body.quote: "An artificial radiation belt could turn a single nuclear detonation into a fleet-wide failure event." (the study's authors, as quoted by Phys.org)

body: Tougher hardware only slowed things down. When the team tripled how much radiation satellites could tolerate, about 97% were still disabled within two weeks, according to the preprint. ScienceAlert reports that a smaller, 100-kiloton blast in the model knocked out about 99% over roughly a year.

Disabled satellites cannot steer out of each other's way. The authors estimate around 20 collisions in the first two years, and ScienceAlert reports some 3,900 new debris fragments after a decade. Replacement satellites would fly straight into the lingering radiation, so restoring services could take years.

This is not purely hypothetical. In 1962 the United States tested a 1.4-megaton warhead, Starfish Prime, about 400 kilometres above the Pacific, and it disabled several of the few satellites then in orbit. The following year the Partial Test Ban Treaty banned nuclear tests in space.

The numbers come from a computer model, and they depend on its assumptions about how much radiation satellites can withstand and how the trapped particles behave. They are best read as an estimate of scale, not a forecast.

headline: Just 403 giant data centres may use nearly as much electricity as an entire US state
dek: A Harvard study estimates that America's largest data centres drew up to 99 terawatt-hours in a year, more than half of it generated from gas and coal.
location: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, United States
body: The cloud is not weightless. A study published on 16 November in Nature Sustainability puts a number on how much power the biggest American data centres, the so-called hyperscale facilities, actually use, and where that power comes from.

Researchers at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, led by postdoctoral fellow Gianluca Guidi with corresponding author Francesca Dominici, found 403 hyperscale centres across the US using a commercial database and satellite imagery. They then estimated each building's yearly electricity use from its size and likely operating hours, for the period May 2024 to April 2025.

Together the 403 facilities used an estimated 68 to 99 terawatt-hours, depending on how hard they were assumed to run. That is about 1.8% of all electricity consumed in the US. The upper estimate comes close to the yearly use of a whole state such as Indiana, Michigan or Tennessee.

body.quote: "It's pretty extraordinary—a few hundred buildings are consuming as much as an entire state." (Gianluca Guidi, Harvard, to National Geographic)

body: Using Environmental Protection Agency data on the power mix serving each facility, the team estimated that about 54% of the electricity came from fossil fuels: 38% from natural gas and 15% from coal. Nuclear supplied around a fifth. That works out to roughly 25.7 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, two to three times an earlier estimate based on 2018 data. About a quarter of the power came from grid regions dirtier than the national average.

The demand is clustered. Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa together accounted for more than half of the electricity used by the facilities studied. Hundreds more hyperscale centres are planned or under construction.

The authors stress that their numbers are estimates, not metered readings. Data were not available for every hyperscale site, and the method cannot separate ordinary cloud computing from AI workloads. Because the building boom has continued since April 2025, Guidi expects today's figures to be higher. The study also did not measure health effects from the extra power-plant pollution; Dominici says that is the team's next step.

Kasparas Spokas of the Clean Air Task Force, who was not involved, told National Geographic the findings should be a wake-up call, since the way new data-centre demand is met will shape power-sector emissions for decades.

headline: Four missing letters of Neanderthal DNA are tied to a smaller visual brain region and lower schizophrenia risk
dek: A variant many people outside Africa still carry sits next to a brain-development gene. Its carriers have slightly smaller occipital lobes and somewhat lower odds of schizophrenia, though nobody yet knows why.
location: Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, Germany
body: Neanderthal skulls were longer and less rounded than ours, which has long hinted that the proportions of their brains differed from modern human brains. A study published on 16 November in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) points to one small piece of Neanderthal DNA that still seems to nudge brain proportions in living people.

The authors are Hugo Zeberg, who works at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig and the Karolinska Institutet in Stockholm, and Svante Pääbo of the Max Planck institute, who won the 2022 Nobel Prize in medicine for sequencing ancient genomes.

body.h2: A tiny deletion with a long history

body: The variant is a deletion of four DNA letters on chromosome 14, close to a gene called DAAM1 that is involved in building the brain. According to ScienceAlert, all five Neanderthal genomes the pair examined carry the deletion, while the two Denisovan genomes do not. The Neanderthal-like stretch of DNA around it is nearly 60,000 letters long, a sign that it arrived through interbreeding rather than being inherited from an older shared ancestor. Today it turns up only in people whose ancestry lies outside sub-Saharan Africa.

Carriers show altered DAAM1 activity. Using genetic and brain data from the UK Biobank, the researchers also found that they have an occipital lobe, the part at the back of the brain that handles vision, about 0.85 cubic centimetres smaller for each copy of the variant. In data from the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, each copy went with roughly 5% lower odds of schizophrenia, and people with two copies had odds almost 10% lower. Neanderthal ancestry as a whole showed no such pattern.

These are statistical associations across large populations, not proof that the variant protects anyone, and the 10% figure is a relative change in odds, not a 10-point drop in an individual's risk. Scientific American reports no link with depression, bipolar disorder or ADHD. Any connection with schooling was tiny or absent: at most about two weeks of education per copy, against an average of around 15 years. The authors write that the results caution against equating the size of a brain region with cognitive ability.

body.quote: "Whether the reduced schizophrenia risk is directly related to the smaller occipital lobe remains, at least for us, unknown." (Hugo Zeberg, speaking to ScienceAlert)

body: There is also a puzzle. Fossil skulls suggest Neanderthals had relatively large occipital regions, so a Neanderthal variant that shrinks this area in modern people is not what one might expect. Zeberg told ScienceAlert that a single variant need not reflect Neanderthal anatomy overall.

Outside researchers were broadly positive but cautious. Nadav Ahituv of the University of California, San Francisco, who reviewed the paper for PNAS, described it to Scientific American as linking an inherited Neanderthal variant to anatomical differences in people today. Speaking to Spain's Science Media Centre, archaeologist Javier Baena of the Autonomous University of Madrid called the work rigorous but said he doubted the schizophrenia effect was statistically meaningful. How the deletion changes DAAM1, and how that might affect the brain, remains to be worked out.

headline: 125,000 years ago, hunters beside a lake in today's Arabian desert may have tipped their weapons with poison
dek: Stone points from the shore of a vanished lake in Saudi Arabia's Empty Quarter carry traces of a toxic plant, alongside bones of hippos, buffalo and camels.
location: Griffith University, Australia, and KAUST, Saudi Arabia
body: The Empty Quarter of southern Arabia is one of the largest sand deserts on Earth. About 125,000 years ago, during a warm and wet spell often called Green Arabia, part of it held a freshwater lake fringed by grassland. A study published in Science describes a campsite on that lake's shore, and some of its stone points may carry the residue of an arrow poison.

The site, 'Uruq Aljelibah, lies on the edge of the ancient Mundafan lake. Terrain models built from satellite data suggest the lake covered about 340 square kilometres and was up to 29 metres deep. The team of 26 researchers was co-led by Chris Clarkson of Griffith University in Australia and Frans van Buchem of King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST), working with Saudi Arabia's Heritage Commission and King Saud University.

From the main excavation the team recovered 5,511 stone tools longer than 2 centimetres, almost all of them flint and made with the Levallois method, in which a stone core is carefully shaped before a flake is struck off. Pieces that fit back together show the tools were made on the spot. Across more than 130 locations the researchers also logged over 500 plant and animal fossils. Remains of hippos, an extinct long-horned buffalo, camels, Arabian oryx, gazelles and ostriches point to animal carcasses being processed at the lake.

Residues turned up on 84% of the stone points examined, and 49% showed signs of having been fixed to a handle or shaft. Some points also carry impact damage of the kind made when a weapon strikes. Chemical traces on several of them match Acokanthera schimperi, a plant known as the arrow poison tree. Other residues came from palms, tubers, shrubs and tree resins, showing that plants were processed too.

body.quote: "Archaeological sites this old rarely preserve such a complete snapshot of daily life." (Chris Clarkson, Griffith University, via IFLScience)

body: The researchers present the poison interpretation as tentative. According to IFLScience, there is no direct evidence that a poisoned weapon brought down any animal, and the team cannot say whether the points tipped thrusting spears or thrown projectiles. The findings also come from a single site.

The paper describes the toolmakers simply as hominins, the group that includes our own species and its close relatives, and places the site within the wider question of how and when Homo sapiens spread out of Africa into Asia. If the poison reading holds up, it would show that people living by Arabia's lost lakes knew their local plants well enough to turn one of them into a weapon.

headline: A tiny brown Florida mushroom makes both a psychedelic and the toxins behind most mushroom deaths
dek: Galerina indica is the first mushroom known to produce psilocybin and amatoxins together. Its genes suggest it borrowed the psychedelic recipe from other fungi.
body: Mushrooms that make psilocybin, the compound behind "magic mushrooms", and mushrooms that make amatoxins, the poisons responsible for most fatal mushroom poisonings, have always been treated as separate groups. A study in Current Biology describes the first species known to make both, and its authors have nicknamed it the dark magic mushroom.

The species is Galerina indica, first described from India in 2015. Researchers led by the University of Florida's Institute of Food and Agricultural Sciences found it in Florida wetlands, growing on a moss-covered palm trunk. It is small and brown, roughly the size of a thumbnail, and looks much like many other species. Matthew Smith, the senior author and Florida's state mycologist, says even trained experts struggle to tell such mushrooms apart.

First author Andrew Kunik, who did the work at the University of Florida, told ScienceAlert that the team cross-checked its results before concluding that both kinds of compound were present. The genus Galerina already includes poisonous species such as the funeral bell, Galerina marginata, which also carries amatoxins.

After sequencing the genome, the team concluded that an ancestor of G. indica could probably already make amatoxins and later picked up the genes for psilocybin through horizontal gene transfer, in which DNA moves between unrelated organisms instead of passing from parent to offspring. A separate Galerina lineage seems to have gained the psilocybin genes in an independent event.

body.quote: "Two independent horizontal gene transfer events for these specialized metabolites in one mushroom genus are unheard of." (Bryn Dentinger, University of Utah, via Popular Science)

body.h2: A warning hidden in a blue bruise

body: Many psilocybin mushrooms stain blue when handled, and some foragers have taken that as a sign a mushroom lacks deadly toxins. G. indica also bruises blue, and the authors write that their finding cautions against reading blue bruising as evidence that amatoxins are absent.

Important gaps remain. The coverage does not report how much of each compound the mushroom contains, so how dangerous it would be to a person is not known. Why a fungus would make both a mind-altering chemical and a lethal one is also unclear; the researchers suggest a mixed chemical defence against animals that eat mushrooms. The specimens are kept at the Natural History Museum of Utah for further testing.

The practical message is simple: nobody should eat wild mushrooms. Small brown mushrooms are notoriously hard to identify, and this one shows that a mushroom with one kind of compound can carry a far more dangerous one as well. Smith says knowing which species grow in a region matters because some can harm people or pets.

headline: After 26 years, the US is officially no longer measles-free
dek: A regional review found that one chain of measles infections kept spreading in the country for more than a year without a break. Mexico and Bolivia lost the same status.
location: Pan American Health Organization, United States
body: The United States has lost the measles elimination status it first earned in 2000. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the World Health Organization's regional office for the Americas, announced the change on 17 November 2026. Mexico and Bolivia lost their status at the same time.

The decision followed a meeting from 10 to 13 November of an independent panel, the Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission. It reviews evidence from 47 countries and territories in the Americas and advises PAHO's director, Jarbas Barbosa, who accepted its recommendations.

Elimination does not mean zero cases. Travellers can still bring the virus in, and outbreaks can still happen. A country only loses the label when a single chain of infections, caused by the same genetic lineage of the virus, keeps spreading without interruption for 12 months or longer.

According to PAHO, the US chain began on 20 January 2025 and crossed the 12-month line on 20 January 2026. Mexico's began on 1 February 2025. Canada lost its own status in November 2025, after an outbreak that started in October 2024, and that loss also cost the Americas as a whole their regional elimination status.

The numbers behind the decision are stark. The CDC counted 5,412 confirmed US cases in 2026 as of 12 November, reported from 47 jurisdictions, with 43 new outbreaks this year. That compares with 2,289 cases in all of 2025. The CDC lists six deaths so far in 2026, while state health officials have reported about 10, a gap IFLScience attributes to the CDC's narrower definition. Across the Americas, PAHO counted 58,213 cases this year.

body.quote: "Elimination is not a trophy that we win once and put on a shelf." (Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director)

body.h2: Can the status be won back?

body: Yes, but it takes time. A country has to stop the endemic chain for at least 12 consecutive months and show that its vaccination, disease surveillance and outbreak response have been strengthened, including a corrective action plan reviewed by the commission. Venezuela and Brazil lost their status in 2018 and 2019 and both had it restored in 2024. Canada declared its outbreak over on 19 October 2026, but it still has to go a full year without spread of that strain.

Vaccination is the main lever. Health officials consider about 95% coverage with two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine necessary to stop spread in every community. Among US kindergarteners in the 2025 to 2026 school year, coverage was 92.4%, according to figures cited by Scientific American, and some states sit far lower.

The label itself changes nothing on the ground: the virus spreads wherever people are unprotected, whatever the official status. Anyone unsure whether they are protected can check their records with a doctor or local health department.

headline: His teeth show a Stone Age Danish fisher's diet changing as the first farmers arrived
dek: Rødhals Man grew up on seafood around 6,000 years ago. From his teens, his meals shifted toward land foods that were probably grown or raised by newly arrived farmers.
body: Around 3900 BC, farming reached Zealand, the largest island in Denmark. For thousands of years before that, people in the region had lived by fishing, hunting and gathering. A study published in the journal Antiquity on 16 November 2026 looks at one man who seems to have lived through the changeover.

He is known as Rødhals Man, after the shell midden, a mound of discarded shells, on the small island of Sejerø where his skeleton was dug up in 1956. A team of 17 researchers led by Anders Fischer of the University of Gothenburg and John Meadows of the Leibniz Centre for Archaeology in Germany re-examined the bones and the excavation records.

body.h2: A life written in layers of tooth

body: Radiocarbon dates, adjusted for the distorting effect of a seafood diet, place his death most likely between about 3890 and 3770 BC. He was about 1.55 metres tall and died between the ages of 30 and 40. His ancient DNA is entirely that of the region's Western Hunter-Gatherers, with no farmer ancestry, and it suggests dark skin and an estimated 85% probability of blue eyes.

To track his meals over time, the team sampled thin, successive layers of dentine inside his teeth, which build up through childhood and adolescence, and measured their chemical isotopes. As a child he ate mostly marine food from shallow coastal waters. From around age 11, more open-sea fish appear. From adolescence onward, the share of protein from land sources rose sharply, which is unusual for coastal foragers of his culture. Because he did not eat freshwater fish, as inland hunters did, the authors argue that the extra land food probably came from farmers.

His grave points the same way. He lay on his back inside a frame of stones, with what may be an archer's wrist guard, a burial style closer to those of early farmers than to typical hunter-gatherer graves of the time. His arm bones show signs of heavy muscle use, possibly from years of paddling.

The researchers are careful about how much one skeleton can say. Bone chemistry alone cannot tell whether he farmed, traded with farmers, or simply hunted more on land. It is also unclear whether he lived mainly on Sejerø or on a bigger island, and the 1956 dig was rushed, so small objects in the grave may have been missed.

body.quote: "It is only one person's story, and only one generation." (Anders Fischer, University of Gothenburg)

body: Still, the find is rare. Hunter-gatherers seem to vanish from the archaeological record in this region almost as soon as farmers appear, which has left open how the two groups met. Rødhals Man suggests that at least some foragers took up parts of the newcomers' way of life while keeping their own ancestry and much of their seafood diet. The team reports a similar pattern in two slightly later individuals from Evensås in western Sweden.

headline: Voyager 1 is now so far away that its signals take a full day to reach us
dek: On 18 November, NASA's 49-year-old probe became the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth. Only two of its science instruments still work, and its power is running down.
location: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, United States
body: NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft passed a symbolic mark on 18 November 2026. At 10:16 UTC (5:16 a.m. EST) it reached one light-day from Earth, a distance of about 25.9 billion kilometres (roughly 16 billion miles). No other human-made object has travelled this far.

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours. A radio command sent from Earth now needs a full day to reach the probe, and any reply needs another day to come back. Voyager project scientist Linda Spilker told Space.com that the probe and Earth are exactly 24 hours apart at the speed of light.

body.h2: Nearly half a century on the road

body: Voyager 1 launched on 5 September 1977, about two weeks after its twin Voyager 2, on a faster path. It flew past Jupiter and Saturn, where its findings included active volcanoes on Jupiter's moon Io. In 2012 it became the first spacecraft to cross into interstellar space, the region beyond the bubble of particles blown out by the Sun. Voyager 2 followed in 2018.

The probe now travels at about 61,000 kilometres per hour and is roughly 173 times farther from the Sun than Earth is, according to ABC News. NASA's Deep Space Network, with large antennas in Canberra, California and Madrid, still tracks it. Voyager 2 is not expected to reach the one-light-day mark until 2035.

The milestone comes as the mission nears its end. Voyager 1 runs on a nuclear power source whose output falls every year. Engineers have switched off almost all of its equipment, including some heaters, and several of its thrusters are clogging. Spilker told ABC News that power and heat should last until about the early 2030s.

Only two of Voyager 1's science instruments still work. Both measure the magnetic field and the charged gas, or plasma, around the probe, and Spilker expects them to stop within about a year. Voyager 2 still has enough power for three instruments. The spacecraft also briefly went silent last month: NASA lost contact with Voyager 1 for about 48 hours before it came back online on its own, before engineers had sent any troubleshooting commands.

body.quote: "They are well past the nine lives of your typical cat. It just keeps going." (Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist, NASA)

body: Bruce Betts, chief scientist of the Planetary Society, who is not part of the mission team, told ABC News that it is unprecedented for a working spacecraft to last this long. Both Voyagers will mark 50 years in space in late 2027. NASA marked the light-day with a public event, asking people to shine a light at the sky and flash the letters V-G-R in Morse code.

headline: Eight teeth suggest Homo erectus lived in China's rainforests far later than thought
dek: Fossil teeth from two caves in Guangxi are dated to between roughly 324,000 and 184,000 years ago, and their chemistry points to a life in dense tropical forest.
body: Homo erectus, an early human species that appeared about two million years ago, is usually pictured striding across open grasslands. Two papers published in Nature on 18 November suggest that at least some of its last populations in mainland Asia lived in dense tropical rainforest instead, and survived there much later than many researchers had assumed.

The work centres on nine hominin teeth from Baxian Cave and Naxian Cave in Guangxi, southern China. Researchers from the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing, Macquarie University and Southern Cross University in Australia, and the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Germany were among those involved.

The first paper identifies eight of the teeth as Homo erectus, based on the shape of the boundary between enamel and dentine inside the teeth and on ancient proteins preserved in them. The ninth, an upper molar from Baxian Cave, has ambiguous features and remains unassigned; one possibility raised is that it belonged to a Denisovan.

The team used five independent dating methods on the teeth and the surrounding cave deposits. The Baxian teeth date to between about 324,000 and 184,000 years ago, and the Naxian teeth to between about 319,000 and 241,000 years ago. That makes them the youngest securely dated Homo erectus fossils from mainland China. Many researchers had thought the species was gone from mainland Asia by around 400,000 years ago.

The second paper looks at chemical signatures in the tooth enamel, along with the teeth of other animals from the caves, which include orangutans and an extinct forest elephant. These signals are consistent with a dense or open-canopy rainforest. Strontium isotopes, which reflect the geology where an individual grew up, suggest that some individuals moved over large distances through the forested limestone landscape, possibly towards what is now northern Vietnam.

body.quote: "The identification looks really solid." (Richard Potts, Smithsonian Institution's Human Origins Program, not involved in the studies, speaking to National Geographic)

body: There are limits. The finds are teeth only, with no skulls or skeletons, and the date ranges are wide, spanning well over 100,000 years. The rainforest interpretation rests on chemical proxies from a small number of individuals. The claims about long-distance movement are framed by the researchers as possibilities.

Even so, the results add to growing evidence that Homo erectus could adapt to very different environments. Why the species eventually disappeared, around 115,000 years ago according to current estimates, remains an open question.

headline: Australia's bogong moths carry a magnetic compass as well as a star compass
dek: Lab experiments show the night-flying moths can steer by the angle of Earth's magnetic field, a trick also used by migrating birds, and that it only works when blue light is present.
body: Every year, huge numbers of bogong moths fly by night across south-eastern Australia to cool caves in the Snowy Mountains, a journey that the research team puts at roughly 1,000 kilometres. In 2025 the same group showed that the moths can hold their course using the stars of the Milky Way. A new study published in Nature on 18 November reports that they also carry a second, independent compass based on Earth's magnetic field.

The work was led by Hui Chen and Eric Warrant at Lund University in Sweden, with colleagues at Carl von Ossietzky University Oldenburg in Germany, the Australian National University and the University of South Australia.

The researchers caught migrating moths with a light trap and tested them in a purpose-built laboratory near Adaminaby in south-eastern Australia, made entirely of non-magnetic materials. Each moth was tethered in a flight arena surrounded by magnetic coils, which let the team change the magnetic field while recording which way the insect tried to fly.

When the field was reversed, the moths turned to match. The key cue was the inclination angle, the angle at which magnetic field lines meet the ground, which grows steeper towards the poles. Birds and sea turtles are known to use the same cue. Filtering out violet and blue light left the moths disoriented, which fits a leading theory that magnetic sensing in animals relies on light-sensitive chemical reactions, possibly involving proteins called cryptochromes.

body.quote: "It is remarkable that two such different groups of animals use the same basic principle to detect Earth's magnetic field." (Eric Warrant, Lund University)

body.h2: Two compasses are better than one

body: The authors suggest that having both a star compass and a magnetic compass could help the moths keep heading the right way when one cue fails, for example under cloudy skies. Insects and birds last shared a common ancestor around 700 million years ago, so the finding hints that similar biological solutions to navigation have evolved, or been kept, in very different lineages.
Ken Lohmann, a sea turtle navigation researcher at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, described the result to National Geographic as fascinating.

The study has limits. The tests were done on tethered moths in a laboratory rather than in free flight over long distances, and the magnetic sensors themselves have not been found. The cryptochrome link is inferred from the light experiments rather than shown directly. The bogong moth is listed as endangered, and researchers hope better knowledge of how it migrates will help protect it.

headline: After a 40-year hunt, CERN physicists see first signs of a one-in-ten-billion decay
dek: The upgraded LHCb detector has found evidence, though not yet proof, that a B meson can decay into two muons at the very rare rate the Standard Model predicts.
body: Physicists at CERN's LHCb experiment have reported the first evidence from a single experiment that a particle called the B0 meson can decay into a pair of muons, heavier cousins of the electron. Theory predicts this happens only about once in every ten billion decays of particles containing a beauty quark, which makes it one of the rarest processes physicists have tried to measure.

The result was announced at a CERN seminar on 3 November 2026. The paper has been posted on the arXiv preprint server and submitted to the journal Physical Review X. It has not yet been peer reviewed.

A B0 meson is made of a beauty quark and a down antiquark. A related particle, the Bs meson, decays into two muons about three times per billion decays. That decay was first observed in 2015 in a joint analysis by LHCb and the CMS experiment. The B0 version is predicted to be about 30 times rarer. The 2015 analysis also hinted at the B0 decay, but later measurements with data up to 2018 did not confirm that hint.

The new analysis is one of LHCb's first to use data from the Large Hadron Collider's third run. It relies on proton collisions recorded in 2024 and 2025 with a detector upgraded in 2024 that can record collisions at up to five times its earlier rate. The team used a machine-learning algorithm to separate the roughly 26 B0 decays expected in that data from a large background of unrelated muon pairs.

The 2024 and 2025 data alone gave a signal at 3.0 standard deviations, or sigma. Combined with LHCb data from 2011 to 2018, the significance rose to 3.2 sigma. Three sigma is the usual bar for calling something "evidence", but particle physicists require five sigma to claim a discovery. The measured rate, about 1.1 per ten billion, matches the Standard Model of particle physics, according to Physics World. The same analysis produced the most precise measurements yet of the Bs decay.

Because these decays are so rare and so precisely predicted, they are a sensitive test for unknown particles that could change the rate. This result does not point to new physics. Instead it narrows the room for theories that would push the rate up or down. LHCb spokesperson Tim Gershon of the University of Warwick told Physics World that the measurements rule out models in which these decay rates would be significantly changed.

body.quote: "The results are very impressive and demonstrate the power of the upgraded LHCb detector" (Robert Fleischer, VU Amsterdam, not involved in the study)

body: The analysis team was led from the UK, with Harry Cliff of the University of Cambridge among its leaders. Reaching five sigma will require more data. LHCb has planned a further upgrade that would increase its data sample by another factor of ten, although Physics World reports that the UK's funding agency withdrew support for UK work on building it in December 2025.

headline: A 3D-printed soft robot with no electronics runs at almost 5 metres per second
dek: Engineers at UC San Diego borrowed a trick from the compound steam engine to make an air-powered, all-soft running robot more than 100 times faster than their earlier design. It still has to be tethered to an air supply.
location: University of California San Diego, United States
body: Soft robots, made from flexible materials rather than metal and motors, are usually slow. A six-legged robot built at the University of California San Diego is a notable exception: it reached a top speed of 4.72 metres per second, which its makers say makes it the fastest robot made entirely of soft materials. The work, by Yichen Zhai and Michael Tolley of UC San Diego's Jacobs School of Engineering, appears in the 18 November 2026 issue of Science Robotics.

The robot is 3D-printed in one piece from a single material and contains no electronics at all. Instead of a computer and motors, it is driven by pressurized air flowing through a network of chambers, valves and tubes printed into its body. That built-in plumbing acts as a fluidic control circuit that tells the legs when to move.

The team's earlier walking robot, first built in 2022, managed only about 4 centimetres per second because its air circuits could not handle much pressure or flow. Running faster meant pushing more air, at higher pressure, through larger and stronger internal structures. But simply venting that high-pressure air after one use wastes much of its energy.

To fix that, the researchers copied the logic of the compound steam engine, in which steam expands through more than one chamber in turn. In the new robot, air passes through twice: first through small high-pressure chambers that run the valves, then through larger low-pressure chambers that move the legs. The paper describes this core as a double-expansion pneumatic oscillator that turns a steady supply of high-pressure gas into four alternating pressure signals at high frequency. The authors estimate the robot's mechanical power output at 169 watts.

body.quote: "Our first walking robot demonstrated what was possible, but it was too slow." (Yichen Zhai, UC San Diego)

body: In tests the robot ran over concrete, gravel, lawn, mulch and sand, ran down stairs, swam, and kept working underwater. The paper also reports that it could be driven with tap water instead of air as the working fluid.

The robot is not yet free-roaming. It works only while connected by a tether to a source of compressed air, such as a conventional compressor. The team says future designs will need to use less air so that a portable source, such as a compressed-air cartridge, could power them, and that steering and grasping objects are also still to come.

The researchers suggest that electronics-free robots like this could eventually be useful where electronics fail, for example in areas with strong radiation or magnetic fields, in disaster response or in space. Those uses have not been demonstrated. We did not find independent expert comment on the study at the time of writing. The work was funded by the US National Science Foundation.

headline: Scientists map 25 million cells in the brain's basal ganglia, a hub tied to Parkinson's and addiction
dek: A package of 26 papers from the NIH-funded BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network builds a cross-species reference map of a deep brain region involved in movement, mood and decision-making.
body: Deep in the brain sits a cluster of structures called the basal ganglia, which help process movement, mood, motivation and decisions. Problems here are linked to conditions ranging from Parkinson's and Huntington's disease to schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and addiction. Researchers have now published what Nature's news team describes as the most detailed atlas of the region so far.

The work appears as a package of 26 peer-reviewed papers in Cell Press journals, including Cell, Cell Reports, Cell Systems, Cell Genomics and Neuron, published on 12 November 2026. It comes from the BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN), a roughly 500-million-dollar effort launched by the US National Institutes of Health in 2022, involving hundreds of scientists at more than 50 institutions in nine countries. The Allen Institute in Seattle, where Hongkui Zeng and Ed Lein helped lead the effort, is among the main contributors.

The atlas profiles 25.5 million cells: 21 million from the brains of six people, 3 million from three macaques and 1.5 million from two marmosets. For each cell the teams measured which genes were active and, in many cases, chemical marks on DNA, electrical activity, how the DNA was folded and where the cell sat in the tissue. Comparing the three primate species, they identified 61 cell types shared across humans, macaques and marmosets.

One study, from Evan Macosko's group at the Broad Institute, examined 1.1 million cells from the striatum, the largest structure in the basal ganglia, taken from 19 deceased donors. Although the striatum has no sharp anatomical borders, the team found six zones with distinct molecular signatures. The differences between zones became less pronounced with age, especially in areas affected by Huntington's and Parkinson's disease.

Other papers in the package link specific cell types to illness. A study in Cell identified a type of striatal neuron, named STR D2 SMYD2-HTR7, associated with higher genetic risk for schizophrenia. A team at the University of California, San Francisco reported genetic changes tied to autism in particular basal ganglia cell types, and a Cell Reports paper described an improved gene therapy approach that reduced tremor in animal models of Parkinson's disease.

body.quote: "It's a massive dictionary that we needed in the field" (Ana Muñoz-Manchado, neuroscientist, University of Cádiz, speaking to Nature)

body: An atlas is a reference tool, not a treatment. The human data come from post-mortem tissue from a limited number of donors, and one study of nearly four million cells from 178 donors found that the cellular make-up of the striatum and prefrontal cortex varied noticeably between people, a reminder that a single map cannot capture everyone. The disease links are associations based on genetics and gene activity, and the Parkinson's gene therapy result was in animals, not people. The data are openly available, and BICAN researchers describe the basal ganglia work as a template for mapping the rest of the brain.
