headline: Why the ground under West Antarctica is rising within decades, not millennia
dek: A new 3D model of the Earth's interior suggests a weak, warm layer of mantle lets the land beneath Thwaites and Pine Island glaciers spring back quickly as the ice above thins.
location: University of Colorado Boulder, United States
body: When a large mass of ice melts, the land underneath slowly rebounds, a bit like a mattress after someone gets up. In most places that process plays out over thousands of years. In parts of West Antarctica, though, satellite and ground instruments show bedrock rising by up to about 5 centimetres a year, much faster than the classic picture would predict.

A study published in Science on 12 November offers an explanation. The team, led by geophysics doctoral candidate Donna dePolo at the University of Colorado Boulder with colleagues including Shijie Zhong and Matt King of the University of Tasmania, built a three-dimensional model of how the mantle beneath West Antarctica flows.

Earlier work had mostly treated the mantle in simpler terms. The new model lets the temperature and stiffness, or viscosity, of the mantle vary with location and depth. The researchers combined it with a reconstruction of Antarctic ice loss from 1900 to 2020, then checked it against GPS measurements of ground motion and gravity changes recorded by the GRACE satellite missions. The calculations were run on a supercomputer in Wyoming.

The model reproduced both the ground motion and the gravity data. According to the paper, a weak layer in the upper mantle, with a viscosity that depends on temperature, fits both the fast rebound seen today and the slow churning of the mantle over millions of years. Some of the fastest uplift is under the Thwaites and Pine Island glaciers, two of the fastest-changing glaciers on the continent.

body.quote: "Rapid ice loss, coupled with a weak upper mantle of the Earth, is allowing this response to happen within decades" (Donna dePolo, University of Colorado Boulder)

body.h2: Why it matters for sea level

body: How quickly the ground rises matters for the ice. Rising bedrock can change how deep the water is where glaciers meet the sea, which affects how fast they retreat. Earlier modelling, including a 2025 study in Nature Communications, has suggested that bedrock uplift could reduce Antarctica's contribution to sea-level rise over the coming centuries. Better models of the solid Earth beneath the ice are needed to make those projections reliable.

The new paper does not itself forecast the future of the ice sheet. Its contribution is a model of the mantle that is consistent with more than a century of reconstructed ice loss and with modern measurements, which other researchers can now build on. The authors also note that the work depends on a small number of research stations in remote parts of Antarctica that track how the crust moves.
The study is peer reviewed. News coverage so far has relied on the authors' own account, and we did not find comment from independent scientists.

headline: Fossil fuel CO2 emissions are set to dip slightly in 2026, but total emissions still hit a record
dek: The annual Global Carbon Budget projects a small fall in emissions from coal, oil and gas this year, mostly because oil use dropped. Fires in south-east Asia mean total emissions are still the highest on record.
body: Carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels and making cement is projected to fall by about 0.4% in 2026, to 38.2 billion tonnes. That is the main finding of the Global Carbon Budget 2026, the 21st yearly assessment by the Global Carbon Project, an international team of more than 140 scientists. The University of Exeter leads it, working with the University of East Anglia, CICERO in Norway, LMU Munich, the Alfred Wegener Institute and many other institutions.
The team describes the figure as a preliminary projection with a wide range. Its estimate runs from a fall of 1.5% to a rise of 0.6%, so the authors say a small increase cannot be ruled out.

Most of the decline comes from oil, where emissions are projected to fall by 1.9%. The researchers link this mainly to the energy shock from the conflict involving Iran, which cut oil use. Gas emissions are projected to fall by 0.3%, while coal emissions are expected to rise by 0.6%.

Country by country, fossil emissions are projected to fall in China (down 0.9%), the United States (down 1.3%), the European Union (down 1.5%) and Japan (down 1%). India is the main exception, with emissions projected to grow by 4.4%. China still produces about 32% of global fossil emissions.

body.h2: Land use pushes the total to a record

body: Emissions from land-use change, such as deforestation, are projected to rise to 5.1 billion tonnes this year, up from 4.4 billion in 2025. The team attributes much of the jump to peat fires and forest degradation in south-east Asia during drier conditions linked to the onset of El Niño. Adding land use to fossil emissions gives a projected record total of 43.3 billion tonnes, slightly above the 42.8 billion tonnes of 2025.

The concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is projected to average 427.7 parts per million in 2026, about 54% above pre-industrial levels. The researchers estimate that 150 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide can still be emitted for a 50% chance of limiting warming to 1.5C, which is less than four years of emissions at the current rate.

body.quote: "A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak unless it is driven by structural change." (Glen Peters, research professor, CICERO)

body: A companion study by the same group in Nature Climate Change estimates that solar power, wind power and electric vehicles offset roughly two thirds of the extra emissions that rising energy demand would otherwise have caused this year. Its authors argue that a lasting peak in global emissions could come within a few years if clean technology keeps spreading faster, but they stress that this year's dip is not yet evidence of such a peak.

There are important limits. The full Global Carbon Budget is published as a preprint in Earth System Science Data and has not yet finished peer review. Estimates for land-use emissions carry much larger uncertainties than those for fossil fuels, and the effect of the developing El Niño on forests and soils is expected to show up mostly in 2027.

headline: Can older people stop their statins? A large trial says it is safe in the short term, but not risk free
dek: In a randomised trial of 1,880 people aged 70 and over without heart disease, stopping statins was judged non-inferior at two years, yet heart attacks, strokes and deaths were more common in those who stopped.
body: Many older adults take a statin for years to lower the chance of a first heart attack or stroke, often alongside a long list of other medicines. Whether they can safely stop has been an open question, because few trials have enrolled people in their late seventies with several chronic illnesses. A new randomised trial called STREAM now offers some of the first direct evidence.

The study, led by Nicolas Rodondi of the Institute of Primary Health Care at the University of Bern, was published in the New England Journal of Medicine and presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions in Chicago. It was funded by the Swiss National Science Foundation.

The trial enrolled 1,880 people aged 70 or older at 24 centres in Switzerland, France and the Netherlands. Their average age was 77.5, just under half were women, and about a third had diabetes. All had at least two chronic conditions, had used a statin for at least a year to prevent a first cardiovascular event, and had no known heart or blood vessel disease. Around 70 percent had been taking a statin for more than six years.

Participants were randomly assigned either to keep taking their statin or to stop it along with any other cholesterol-lowering drug. The main measure was the first occurrence of a non-fatal heart attack, a non-fatal ischaemic stroke or death from any cause.

At two years, the stopping strategy met the trial's pre-set test of non-inferiority. People who stopped spent an average of 96.5 weeks free of a major event, compared with 98.5 weeks for those who continued, a gap of two weeks that fell inside the allowed margin of 5.2 weeks. Rodondi estimated that for every 40 people who stopped, there was one additional major cardiovascular event or death over two years.

Over the full follow-up of up to four years (median 103 weeks), the difference grew clearer. A primary-outcome event occurred in 12.7 percent of people who stopped versus 9.2 percent of those who continued. Heart attacks occurred in 1.6 versus 0.6 percent, ischaemic strokes in 2.2 versus 0.8 percent and deaths in 9.8 versus 8.0 percent. Serious adverse events were reported in 43 percent of the stopping group and 39.8 percent of the continuing group.

The hoped-for benefits of stopping did not clearly appear. The researchers found no meaningful differences between groups in quality of life, pain, falls, risk of muscle loss or adherence to other medicines. In June 2026 the trial's independent safety monitoring board advised that people in the stopping group discuss restarting statins with their doctors.

STREAM was open label, so participants and doctors knew who had stopped, and the results apply only to people without known cardiovascular disease. The authors note that changes in other preventive medicines during follow-up could have influenced the results, and they call for more trials of stopping specific drugs. Rodondi said the small rise in risk means no general recommendation to stop statins can be made for this group.

body.quote: "We should certainly not rush to stop statins based on this, but we should talk with our patients about their priorities." (Karen Alexander, Duke Clinical Research Institute, discussant at the AHA meeting)

body: Others were more cautious still. Dinesh Kalra of the University of Louisville, speaking in a personal capacity, told TCTMD that people who tolerate statins should keep taking them because those who stop will have more heart attacks and strokes over time. For now, the trial gives doctors and older patients numbers to weigh together rather than a simple rule.

headline: A virtual copy of the Webb telescope found a planet that old images had missed
dek: By simulating Webb's camera in detail and subtracting the star's glare, astronomers made the telescope 2 to 15 times more sensitive to faint planets in archival data.
body: Photographing a planet around another star is hard because the star's glare swamps the planet's faint light. Astronomers at Northwestern University now report a way to clean up that glare in software. Applied to observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), their method picked out a giant planet that standard processing could not separate from the leftover starlight.

The study, titled "Imaging exoplanets below the telescope stability limit", was published in Nature on 4 November 2026. It was led by Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, a PhD student in astronomy at Northwestern, working in the group of physicist and astronomer Jason Wang.

Webb's NIRCam camera uses a coronagraph, a mask that blocks most of a star's light. Some glare always leaks through, and it shifts slightly as the telescope wobbles and its optics change by tiny amounts. The team's method, called FLIP (Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets), builds a detailed simulation, or "digital twin", of how starlight travels through the telescope to the detector.

The researchers tuned millions of settings in the model until it matched the real telescope's small flaws, such as slight shifts in position and optical distortions. They then subtracted the simulated glare from the real images. Wang said the team used the same computer tools that are used to train AI models, but the method itself does not use AI to find planets.

body.quote: "It is something like an artificial eclipse." (Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, Northwestern University, describing the coronagraph)

body: The team reanalysed archival Webb observations of three stars: HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani, both of which have known planets, and TYC 5899, which has none. FLIP was 2 to 15 times more sensitive to faint planets than standard techniques, with the biggest gains close to the star. In roughly two-year-old data of 51 Eridani, taken at a wavelength of 4.3 microns where carbon dioxide absorbs strongly, it detected the giant planet 51 Eridani b with a significance above 5 sigma, a common threshold for a confident signal.

There are clear limits. 51 Eridani b was discovered years ago with ground-based telescopes, so this is a test of the method rather than the discovery of a new world. The work used only three archival targets, and the model has to be tuned to each set of observations before it can remove the glare.

Dimitri Mawet, a senior research scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory who was not involved in the study, called it "a significant result" in Scientific American. He said such physics-based processing could ease part of the extreme stability requirements of NASA's proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory, a future telescope meant to image Earth-like planets that is slated to launch in the 2040s. Imaging Earth-sized worlds would need a telescope 100 to 1,000 times more stable than Webb.

headline: Heat was linked to a record 710,000 deaths in 2023, says the tenth Lancet Countdown report
dek: The annual climate and health report estimates that heat-related deaths have risen sharply since the Paris Agreement, and its authors want climate change recognised as a global health emergency.
body: Every year, a large international team tracks how climate change is affecting human health and how well the world is responding. The tenth edition of this report, the Lancet Countdown on health and climate change, was published in The Lancet on 28 October 2026, ahead of the COP31 climate summit. It was produced by 146 researchers led from University College London, working in collaboration with the World Health Organization.
The report follows 54 indicators, four of them new this year, covering everything from heat and infectious disease to air pollution, food security and money spent on fossil fuels.

Its headline estimate is that about 710,000 deaths worldwide were linked to heat in 2023, the hottest year in the period studied and the highest toll the team has recorded. The authors attribute 71.5 percent of those deaths to human-caused climate change.

Across 2016 to 2023, heat was linked to an average of about 540,800 deaths a year, around 36 percent more than in the previous decade. The share attributed to climate change rose from 55 percent to about 68 percent. Marina Romanello, the Countdown's executive director at UCL, summed this up as roughly three million heat-related deaths in the eight years since the 2015 Paris Agreement.

body.quote: "That's roughly equivalent to the entire population of Wales being wiped out in the space of eight years due to heat" (Marina Romanello, executive director, Lancet Countdown, speaking to AFP)

body.h2: Other warning signs, and some progress

body: The report also estimates that heat cost about 573 billion working hours and roughly 1.07 trillion US dollars in lost income in 2025, and that dengue reached a record 14.4 million cases in 2024. It found that 71 percent of WHO member states had no plan, as of 2025, for adapting their health systems to climate change.

Not every trend was negative. The authors point to rising investment in clean energy, which AFP reported reached 2.1 trillion US dollars in 2025, about double the amount invested in fossil fuels, and to falling air pollution from fossil fuels in dozens of countries since 2016. But they say progress has been too slow and uneven, and that political attention to climate and health has fallen, with health-and-climate mentions in UN General Debate speeches dropping sharply since 2021.

On that basis the authors call for climate change to be formally recognised as a global health emergency and for a new WHO instrument to coordinate the response. This is a recommendation from the report's authors, not a declaration by WHO.

The death figures are modelled estimates rather than a count of individual death certificates, so they carry statistical uncertainty. Romanello told AFP that this year's work was complicated by the disappearance of some data sources, particularly in the United States, where some fossil-fuel subsidy data have not been made public. Most of the experts quoted in coverage are themselves part of the Countdown collaboration, so the report is best read as a large, structured synthesis rather than an independent verdict.

headline: Brown engineers keep a magnetic-electric material working at just a few atoms thick
dek: Multiferroic films usually lose their useful properties when made thin enough for chips. A Brown University team reports in Nature Materials a way to avoid that, and finds the films become an unusual kind of magnet.
body: Some materials, called multiferroics, are both electrically polarized and magnetic, and the two properties are linked. That makes them attractive for computer memory and logic: a small voltage could flip the electrical state to write a bit, and the linked magnetic state could be used to read it back, potentially using far less energy than today's devices.

There has long been a catch. When multiferroic films are made thin enough to be useful in a chip, they tend to stop working. Below a certain thickness the crystal structure loses the shape it needs, and internal electric fields swamp the material's polarization, leaving a so-called dead layer that is neither ferroelectric nor magnetic.

A team led by Lucas Caretta, an assistant professor of engineering at Brown University, reports in Nature Materials that it has found a way around the problem in bismuth ferrite, one of the most widely studied multiferroics. The paper was published online on 28 October 2026.

The researchers grew bismuth ferrite films on a substrate of dysprosium scandate, a rare-earth compound whose crystal spacing is slightly smaller. That mismatch squeezes the film and helps it keep its working atomic structure. A second, metallic layer soaks up the stray electric fields that would otherwise destroy the polarization.

body.quote: "We've established that we can get rid of the dead layer." (Lucas Caretta, Brown University)

body: According to Brown, the films stayed ferroelectric and magnetic down to thicknesses of a few angstroms, and their magnetic behavior was actually enhanced. The team's earlier preprint of the work describes the films reaching a thickness of four crystal unit cells, and says the conclusions rest on a combination of theoretical calculations, symmetry analysis, atomic-resolution imaging and several magnetic measurements.

The researchers also report signatures of altermagnetism in the ultrathin films. Altermagnets are a recently recognized class of magnetic materials that sit between ferromagnets, whose strong signals are easy to read but whose stray fields make dense packing hard, and antiferromagnets, which are fast and produce no stray fields but are hard to read. Caretta argues that altermagnets could offer speed, dense packing and a readable signal together.

The study does not report a working memory chip or any measured energy savings; the low-power benefits are a goal rather than a result. Caretta describes the work as a step toward low-power computing, and ScienceDaily's account notes that more development is needed before such films could be manufactured reliably and built into commercial electronics. We did not find independent expert comment on the paper at the time of writing. The work was funded by the US Army Research Office, the National Science Foundation and the Department of Energy.
